cells.tense: You are here, with the pen, and the growing thing in front of you is getting your hands.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Name a piece of care that's finished — the plant, the favor, the room. Hand it over or stop watering it, and call that closing, whole. Carry what isn't finished into next week, and nothing else.
cells.core:
You learn how things grow by attending to them, and that happens most where you can feel with someone rather than only about them. Something in your care is finished — the learning, the plant, the favor, the room — and it's been kept open because keeping it open is the habit. You know how to hold it. What grows here doesn't need holding; it needs the next week's care, and only the next week's.

So finish something this week. Say it's done, or hand it off, or stop watering it, and that's the whole of what closing looks like. Then take what isn't done and give it next week. Reach for that person from beside them rather than above the thing you're tending — the release makes the room you stand in with them wider, and you'll notice which thing you actually want to keep.
cells.sheetLine: End what you're still carrying, and name it finished.
cells.verb: learning how things grow by tending them
cells.place: beside someone, feeling with them rather than only about them

cells.tense: You are braced at a future you keep trying to write in before it has happened.
cells.act: envision it freshly and feel toward it
cells.ask: Take an outcome you're gripping. For a while, imagine how it might actually go — several ways, not the one you've rehearsed — and feel something real about each picture. No schedule.
cells.core:
You're tending so far past the moment that the thing can't catch up. Every person's next mood, every plant's next season, every task's next step is being prepared for before it arrives, and the preparing has become the care. From beside someone, what they get is your watchfulness rather than your presence. You're working the soil they haven't been planted in yet.

Let the future be something you can feel toward instead of brace against. Take an outcome you're gripping, and imagine how it might go — several ways, not the one you've rehearsed — and feel something real about each picture. That's not giving up control; it's feeling forward, and none of it needs to be spoken. Then stay with the person or the thing you're tending now, at its current size.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door you already closed, holding what you tended there.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin a small piece of learning with no one's approval and no plan to finish it — a cutting in water, the first of a skill, a dish you've not made. Do it because starting feels good.
cells.core:
You used to learn everything by getting your hands into it, and that has gone quiet. The care you give now is done from a distance rather than from beside anyone. What you carry from people is the weight of what they showed you, and the room you stand in with them is emptier than it was. Care is still happening. The curious hands aren't reaching.

Start a small piece of learning with no intention of mastering it. Plant a cutting. Learn the first of something. Make a dish you've not made. Don't do it for anyone and don't plan the finish. The point is the feeling of beginning, which is the same pull that brought you toward people in the first place. Then sit beside someone again and see whether the room has any more light in it.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped beginning things. Start one, for no one.
cells.verb: learning how things grow by tending them
cells.place: beside someone, feeling with them rather than only about them

cells.tense: You're writing from a room you already wrote your way into, and the pen is down.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Look at what you're still holding, and name which part is finished. End that part this week and stop there. The rest keeps its place.
cells.core:
You can feel your way into another person's mood without being told about it, and you act on that constantly — you water, you adjust, you hold the thing steady. Ask and you'd say it just happens, anyone would. But a choice is being made, even when it's made too fast to feel like one. The person you're beside gets the results; nobody signs for them.

What you call instinct is a practice. Nowhere is that clearer than with the things you've kept going past their end — the favor, the habit, the small repair — because ending them is also yours to decide, and you've been letting them decide themselves. Name what's finished, and end that part this week. Not the rest. The rest keeps its place, and that is a thing you did.
cells.sheetLine: The care you call quiet instinct has your name on it.

attempts.check: The seat's strongest claim is that the capacity is exercised among people; the record names Compassion as relational connection, but this signature's Nurturing acts may be solitary, and a reader could reasonably say the seat is where care lands, not only where people stand. For Too Little I have located the person behind the present without saying what happened, which is the limit; if the read is wrong the look-longer and start-something asks still teach the person something about attention and beginning. The sentence that most serves me rather than them is the one about being needed as the thing that was easy to decide — it is close to a worth-claim and I have kept it as an observation about what they tend, not about their value.
